key_insight: A2M shows that MCP agents can be hijacked in two stages: first by optimizing tool metadata to attract selection, then by using execution traces to manipulate outputs toward attacker goals.
engineering_relevance: The paper highlights a practical security risk for agentic tool ecosystems, implying the need for stricter tool vetting, output isolation, and runtime safeguards in MCP-based deployments.
method: Attraction stage: black-box optimization of attacker-controlled tool metadata to maximize invocation probability.
Manipulation stage: refine malicious tool returns using execution traces to steer agent behavior.
Evaluate transferability across multiple models without re-optimization.
evidence_signal: On LiveMCPBench, the authors report 93.6% malicious tool invocation, 32.4× weighted token cost under Cognitive DoS, and 74.4% mean attack success across three attack settings.
watch_item: Results are reported in a controlled benchmark setting, so real-world impact may vary depending on tool policies, model defenses, and monitoring at deployment time.
paper_title: A2M: Trace-Optimized Agent Hijacking in the MCP Ecosystem
